concept.name: Circuit breaker
concept.definition: A system of coordinated trading halts and/or price limits on equity and equity-derivative markets designed to provide a cooling-off period during large intraday market declines; the term entered regulation via the 1988 Brady Report recommendations after the October 1987 crash. In U.S. equities, market-wide circuit breakers halt all markets when the S&P 500 falls 7%, 13%, or 20% from the prior close.
concept.intuition: When the whole market falls too far too fast, everything stops for a set period so panic cannot feed on itself uninterrupted.
concept.mechanics: Market-wide circuit breakers trigger cross-market halts at S&P 500 declines of 7% (Level 1) and 13% (Level 2) before 3:25 p.m. ET, each pausing trading for 15 minutes; a 20% decline (Level 3) halts trading for the remainder of the day. Single-stock analogues operate through Limit Up-Limit Down price bands.
concept.failure_modes: Critics note 'magnet effects' — traders rush to sell ahead of a trigger, accelerating the very decline the rule targets — and halts merely delay, rather than prevent, repricing to new information.
concept.misconceptions: Circuit breakers do not stop losses or stabilize fundamentals; they only pause trading. They also rarely trigger: market-wide halts are extreme events, not routine safeguards.
concept.example: On four days in March 2020, the S&P 500 fell 7% shortly after the open, triggering Level 1 market-wide circuit breakers that halted all U.S. equity trading for 15 minutes.

citations.source: SEC, Market Volatility Procedures and Circuit Breakers (Investor.gov)
citations.section: Circuit breakers and market volatility procedures
